title: Kernel scheduling entropy profile and memory-bandwidth correlation
body:
Summary:
This note describes an exploratory profiling run focused on how kernel scheduling 'entropy' (irregular ordering and spacing of kernel launches) correlates with observable drops in achieved memory bandwidth and effective occupancy for our microbatch inference workload (gpt-medium-ish, kv-cache heavy). The goal was to find whether irregular CUDA graph fragment boundaries and async memcpy phasing reduce sustained DRAM throughput and to propose mitigations for tail-latency and cost regressions.

Motivation and context:
- Recent production rollout on Dedicated showed a ~7-12% token-cost increase under mixed small/large request mixes.
- Preliminary traces flagged intermittent memory-bandwidth collapses that coincide with series of short kernels and repeated tiny memcpys.
- Hypothesis: scheduler-level fragmentation (many tiny kernels + async copies) increases SM idle time and prevents sustained memory pipeline fill, reducing measured bandwidth and driving per-token latency up.

Testbed and capture parameters:
- HW: A100-80GB instances (p3dn-like), driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.0
- Models: open-gpt-7b-quantized (fp16+4bit), context window trimmed to 2k tokens for stress runs
- Workloads: microbatch sizes {1,2,4} with interleaved long and short requests to emulate PLG traffic
- Batchers: continuous-batcher with and without CUDA graph replay (graph fragment size varied)
- Tools: NVTX annotations, nv-nsight-cu-cli timeline capture, nvprof (select counters), CUPTI-derived bandwidth monitor
- Nsight capture flags used: --timeline --metrics sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak,smm__pipe_lsu_avg.active,dram__throughput.avg
- Repro commands (high-level):
  - start capture: nv-nsight-cu-cli --target-processes all --timeline --metrics dram__throughput.avg --output timeline.qdrep -- <runner>
  - capture slices: nvprof --profile-from-start off --print-gpu-trace --metrics achieved_occupancy,inst_executed

Key observations (representative run):
- Run A (no cuda-graph): sustained DRAM throughput ~450 GB/s for long kernels; bursty dips to ~120-160 GB/s during sequences of 8-12 short kernels (duration <250us), corresponding to a ~18% drop in average tokens/sec over the trace window.
- Run B (cuda-graph full-replay, large fragments): fewer short-kernel gaps, DRAM throughput steadier (~470 GB/s sustained), but heavier peak-power usage and one-off SM saturation spikes.
- Run C (cuda-graph with small fragments + async memcpy interleaving): observed repeated re-warming periods. After an async memcpy completes, first kernel often shows ~30-50% lower SM active fraction for ~200-400us before ramping back. This ramp correlated with KV cache touch patterns.
- Kernel ordering entropy metric: we computed a simple entropy score per capture by hashing the sequence of kernel names and memcpy types over fixed windows; high-entropy windows (>1.8 bits kernel-shuffle score) matched the low-bandwidth valleys.

Microbenchmarks to isolate causes:
1) Tiny-kernel chain: launch 40 no-op kernels (each ~30us) back-to-back and measure dram__throughput. Result: pipeline starvation observed; throughput collapsed to ~25% of single large-kernel baseline.
2) Async memcpy spacing: issue 4 async copies interleaved with tiny kernels; vary stream priorities. Result: using high-priority stream for memcpy reduced re-warm delay by ~60% vs equal priority, but increased interference for compute-heavy kernels if not carefully pinned.
3) KV-cache touch pattern: simulate KV reads across large cache lines after idle period. Cold reads introduced a latency tail and initial DRAM bandwidth spike followed by immediate drop for small kernels.

Timeline and kernel-level details (nsight snippets paraphrased):
- Timeline slice (example):
  t=0ms: async memcpy H2D (48KB) -> peak dram 600GB/s for 40us
  t=0.05ms: kernel A (matmul shard) launch -> sm_active 65% -> dram 480GB/s
  t=0.30ms: kernel B (softmax tiny) launch -> sm_active 22% -> dram 140GB/s
  t=0.36ms: kernel C (kv read) launch -> sm_active 28% -> dram 160GB/s
  repeated pattern leads to moving average drop

Interpreting the signals:
- Short kernels (under ~200-300us) don't keep DMA engines fully utilized; combined with small, frequent async memcpy they create windows where global DRAM demand is too fragmented to sustain device-level prefetch/row-buffer locality.
- CUDA graph replay helps by consolidating launches into fewer submit events (reduces launch overhead and scheduler jitter). However, small graph fragments still permit fragmentation inside the device scheduler which doesn't merge memory accesses across fragment boundaries.
- Stream priority tuning helps reduce memcpy-induced stalls if memcopies are on the same device and using peer2peer paths; but it can cause compute starvation if not balanced.

Short quantitative summary (representative):
- Avg tokens/sec: baseline 1.00x, fragmented small-kernel mix 0.86x, large-fragment cuda-graph 1.06x
- Measured avg dram throughput: baseline 470 GB/s, fragmented 300 GB/s, cuda-graph-large 490 GB/s
- Tail (95th) token latency: baseline 210ms, fragmented 280ms, cuda-graph-large 195ms

Hypotheses and next experiments:
- Hypothesis 1: Merging kernels at the launcher level into fewer, slightly larger cuGraph fragments should allow device memory controllers to sustain higher throughput. Experiment: synthetic fusion of small kernels into combined kernels (prototype in local runner).
- Hypothesis 2: Introducing a short busy-wait microkernel to keep DMA engines active across fragment boundaries could bridge the re-warm gap. Experiment: trampoline kernel (very cheap compute) inserted after memcpy to prime memory pipelines.
- Hypothesis 3: KV cache access pattern change (striped reads rather than many tiny reads) improves row-buffer locality. Experiment: batch KV reads into coalesced blocks where possible.

Action items and tactical mitigations:
- Implement dynamic cuda-graph fragment sizing: if the sampler detects a high-kernel-entropy window, grow fragment size to reduce submission jitter. (Owner: Ethan)
- Add optional post-memcpy microkernel primer (config flag) to test re-warm benefit with controlled overhead (Owner: Liang)
- Add telemetry metric to runner: kernel-entropy-score and short-kernel-fraction per second to correlate with cost spikes. Surface in Console Optimize dashboards. (Owner: Product/Telemetry)
- Run controlled A/B on Dedicated pool with fragment-sizing enabled for 48-72 hours to measure cost and tail effects before rolling to broader traffic.

Open questions and risks:
- Power/thermal tradeoffs: cuda-graph-large increases steady-state power — will this impact Dedicated SLA/cost? Need SRE input.
- Interactions with multi-tenant P2P/IPC: our experiments were on isolated devices. Peer access patterns in co-located environments may amplify or reduce the effect.
- Verification on other HW: need to run same captures on H100-like hardware; memory subsystem behavior differs and could change the recommendations.

Appendix: quick commands and notes
- nv-nsight capture tip: capture full timeline but limit capture windows to ~200ms slices to keep qdrep sizes manageable. Use --processes all to ensure memcpy visibility.
- Quick compute to derive entropy score (rough): map kernel name -> small ordinal, take sliding window of 32 events, compute Shannon entropy of ordinal distribution; threshold empirically at >1.6 for problematic windows.
- Sample nvprof metric set used: achieved_occupancy, inst_executed, dram_read_transactions, dram__throughput.avg

Conclusion:
We have an actionable signal linking kernel launch fragmentation and async-copy phasing to drops in sustained DRAM throughput and occupancy. Short-term mitigations (graph fragment resizing, memcpy stream priority, primer kernel) are low-risk to prototype and should be validated in a controlled Dedicated run. Longer-term: incorporate kernel-entropy telemetry and an optimizer that adaptively restructures graph fragments to workload shape.

Notes-to-self (loose):
- Save a small replay script for tracer reproducibility (nsight repro commands) and attach to Jira ticket.
